traditions.name: Ancient Chinese state religion (Shang–Zhou)
traditions.scholarly_note: Shang divination inscriptions name Di / Shangdi as the high power; the Zhou court (from c. 1046 BCE) fused Di with Tian (Heaven). Later imperial state ritual continued both names.

traditions.name: Japanese Buddhism and syncretic folk religion (shinbutsu-shūgō)
traditions.scholarly_note: Covers the Japanese forms of Indian and Chinese Buddhist deities (Kannon, Jizō, Enma, the deva-guardians) and the Edo-period Seven Lucky Gods, which mix Buddhist, Daoist and Shinto figures.

traditions.name: Tagalog anitism (pre-colonial Philippine religion)
traditions.scholarly_note: Known chiefly through Spanish-era accounts (Juan de Plasencia, 1589; the Boxer Codex, c. 1590; Pedro Chirino, 1604) and 20th-century folklore compilations. Several family relationships among the deities circulate only in the later compilations.

traditions.name: Visayan anitism
traditions.earliest_attestation: late 16th c. CE (Miguel de Loarca, Relación, 1582)
traditions.scholarly_note: Known from Spanish-era accounts (Loarca 1582; Alcina 1668) and living oral tradition.

traditions.name: Balinese Hinduism (Agama Hindu Dharma)
traditions.scholarly_note: A distinct Hindu-Buddhist-indigenous synthesis. The monotheistic framing around Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa was formalised by the Parisada Hindu Dharma Indonesia from 1959 within Indonesia's Pancasila framework.

traditions.name: Javanese religion (Kejawen and wayang cosmology)
traditions.earliest_attestation: c. 9th–10th c. CE (Old Javanese inscriptions and kakawin)

traditions.name: Ngaju Dayak religion (Kaharingan)
traditions.scholarly_note: Kaharingan was officially registered in 1980 under the Hindu umbrella in Indonesia; the Ngaju priestly chants are its main sources.

traditions.name: Toba Batak religion (Parmalim and older tradition)
traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition and pustaha bark books; recorded 19th c. CE

traditions.name: Malay folk religion (keramat cult)
traditions.scholarly_note: The keramat shrine cult blends Sufi saint veneration with older Malay guardian-spirit belief and is shared by Chinese Malaysians as Datuk Gong.

traditions.name: Burmese nat worship
traditions.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (court pantheon traditionally fixed under King Anawrahta)
traditions.scholarly_note: Burmese royal chronicles (Maha Yazawin, 18th c.; Hmannan Yazawin, 1832) preserve the official list of Thirty-Seven Nats, headed by Thagyamin.

traditions.name: Tai / Lao spirit religion (satsana phi)
traditions.scholarly_note: Coexists with Theravada Buddhism; spirit houses, guardian spirits and rice-spirit rites form a continuous layer beneath and around Buddhist practice.

traditions.name: Tahitian / Society Islands religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 18th–19th c. CE
traditions.scholarly_note: Principal published collection: Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928), compiled from her grandfather J. M. Orsmond's 19th-century notes.

traditions.name: Rapa Nui religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition, petroglyphs at ʻOrongo; recorded 19th–20th c. CE

traditions.name: Cook Islands religion (Mangaia)
traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded 19th c. CE (W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, 1876)

traditions.name: Fijian religion
traditions.scholarly_note: Fiji sits at the Melanesia–Polynesia boundary; Degei and the Kalou-vu (ancestor gods) are its best-documented figures.

traditions.name: Aboriginal Australian (pan-continental motifs)
traditions.earliest_attestation: rock art of great antiquity; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
traditions.scholarly_note: Used only for cross-regional groupings such as the Rainbow Serpent, a term coined by anthropologists for many distinct, Country-specific beings. Drawn only from published, publicly available (non-restricted) material; restricted and secret-sacred knowledge is deliberately excluded. Authority over these narratives rests with the custodians of the relevant Country, and versions differ between language groups.

traditions.name: Aboriginal — Southwest (Noongar)
traditions.scholarly_note: Drawn only from published, publicly available (non-restricted) material; restricted and secret-sacred knowledge is deliberately excluded. Authority over these narratives rests with the custodians of the relevant Country, and versions differ between language groups.

traditions.name: Aboriginal — Tiwi Islands
traditions.geographic_origin: Bathurst and Melville Islands, Northern Territory
traditions.scholarly_note: Drawn only from published, publicly available (non-restricted) material; restricted and secret-sacred knowledge is deliberately excluded. Authority over these narratives rests with the custodians of the relevant Country, and versions differ between language groups.

traditions.name: Torres Strait Islander religion
traditions.scholarly_note: The Malo-Bomai cult of Mer (Murray Island) is documented in the Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits (vol. 6, 1908). Only published, non-restricted material is used.

primary_sources: Sima Zhen, supplement to the Shiji
deities.etymology: Possibly "hidden breath" / "subduer of animals"; also written 庖犧 Paoxi, "sacrificial kitchen".
iconography: serpent lower body entwined with Nüwa
deities.summary: First of the Three Sovereigns. Fuxi looked up at the patterns of heaven and down at the forms of earth and drew the Eight Trigrams; he taught people to knot nets, hunt, fish and marry. With his sister-consort Nüwa he is the serpent-bodied ancestral pair who hold the compass and set-square of cosmic order.

deities.earliest_attestation: 6th–10th c. CE (Chinese Buddhist translation; Scripture on the Ten Kings, c. 9th–10th c.)
primary_sources: Scripture on the Ten Kings (Shiwang jing)
Chinese Buddhist sutra translations of Yama
deities.etymology: Chinese transliteration of Sanskrit Yama-rāja (閻羅王).
deities.summary: Yanluo Wang is the Yama King, ruler of the Fifth Court of Diyu. Every soul stands before him after death; in his mirror of karma it sees its own deeds, and he assigns it to punishment or rebirth. Once ruler of the First Court, he was demoted to the Fifth for being too merciful to the dead.

deities.etymology: 上帝 "the high/supreme Di"; Di may originally have denoted the ancestral sacrifice or a royal ancestor.
deities.summary: Shangdi, the Lord on High, commands wind, rain, thunder and harvest and decides the fate of the kingdom and its wars. Royal ancestors stand in his presence and intercede for their descendants. Under the Zhou he is one with Heaven (Tian), and to the end of the empire the Son of Heaven sacrificed to Huangtian Shangdi at the winter solstice.

deities.earliest_attestation: Song–Yuan period (c. 12th–14th c. CE) Daoist scriptures
primary_sources: Daoist Canon (Daozang) scriptures of the Dipper Mother
iconography: three heads, eight or more arms
deities.summary: Doumu is the Mother of the Dipper, who gave birth to the nine stars of the Northern Dipper that govern every life's length and fate. Many-armed and many-eyed, holding sun and moon, she sits at the pole of heaven; those who recite her scripture can have the records of death erased.

deities.earliest_attestation: Tang period (7th–8th c. CE) as a fixed triad; components 4th–6th c. CE
deities.summary: The Three Pure Ones are the highest emanations of the Dao: Yuanshi Tianzun of the Jade Purity, Lingbao Tianzun of the Upper Purity and Daode Tianzun (the deified Laozi) of the Great Purity. They are the primordial breath divided into three heavens, from which every lower god, scripture and teaching flows.

Yuanshi Tianzun, the Celestial Worthy of Primordial Beginning, existed before heaven and earth. In each cosmic cycle he reveals the sacred scriptures, written in self-generated celestial script, to the lesser gods, who pass them down to humanity.

Lingbao Tianzun, the Celestial Worthy of the Numinous Treasure, is the second of the Three Pure Ones. He holds the cosmic balance of yin and yang and keeps the sacred scriptures and talismans, mediating them from the primordial to the created world.

primary_sources: Yuan drama of the Eight Immortals
deities.summary: Lü Dongbin is the best loved of the Eight Immortals, a scholar who failed the examinations, woke from the Yellow Millet Dream and learned inner alchemy from Zhongli Quan. With his demon-slaying sword he roams the world healing, testing and teaching, and he still descends in spirit-writing to instruct his followers.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ming period (16th c. CE; Zhao Gongming in the Fengshen yanyi)
primary_sources: Lunar New Year popular prints and liturgies
deities.summary: Caishen, the God of Wealth, is welcomed into every home on the fifth day of the New Year. As the martial Zhao Gongming riding a black tiger he guards and gathers riches; as the civil Bigan or Fan Li he bestows prosperity on the upright.

deities.earliest_attestation: by 6th c. CE; state cult codified 1369 CE (Ming Hongwu)
deities.summary: Chenghuang, the God of Walls and Moats, is the magistrate of the unseen world for each city. Usually a just official of the past appointed by Heaven, he keeps the registers of the living and dead, arrests wandering ghosts and reports to the courts of the underworld, mirroring the human magistrate who governs by day.

deities.earliest_attestation: Song period (10th–11th c. CE; Guankou cult in Sichuan)
deities.summary: Erlang Shen, the Second Son, is the god with a third eye in his forehead and the Howling Celestial Dog at his side. At Guankou he tamed the floods of the Min River; in heaven he is the warrior who matched Sun Wukong transformation for transformation and captured him.

alternate_names: Dragon Kings of the Four Seas
deities.earliest_attestation: Tang period (7th–9th c. CE); imperial titles under the Song
deities.summary: The Dragon Kings rule the Four Seas and every river, lake and well. They bring the rain at Heaven's command, and villagers pray at their temples in drought. Ao Guang of the Eastern Sea, Ao Qin, Ao Run and Ao Shun keep crystal palaces beneath the waves.

deities.earliest_attestation: Han period (1st–2nd c. CE; bronze mirrors and tomb reliefs)
deities.summary: Dongwanggong, King Father of the East, is the yang partner of the Queen Mother of the West. He keeps the registers of the male immortals in the east as she keeps the female immortals in the west; together they balance the cosmos.

deities.earliest_attestation: early 16th c. CE (baojuan "precious scrolls" of Luo Qing's sect, 1509)
primary_sources: Baojuan (precious scrolls) of the Luo and later sectarian traditions
deities.summary: The Eternal Venerable Mother is the unborn source of all souls. Her children fell into the world of dust and forgot their true home; she weeps for them and sends Maitreya and her messengers so that all may return to the True Emptiness Native Land at the end of the age.

primary_sources: Shiji (Basic Annals of the Five Emperors)
deities.summary: Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, is the ancestor of the Chinese people and first of the Five Emperors. He defeated Chiyou at Zhuolu, gave the arts of medicine, the calendar, writing and silk through his ministers and consort, and at the end ascended to heaven on a dragon.

deities.earliest_attestation: Warring States period (4th c. BCE; Mencius)
primary_sources: Shennong bencao jing (Divine Farmer's Materia Medica)
deities.summary: Shennong, the Divine Farmer, taught humanity to plough and sow the five grains. He tasted a hundred herbs in one day, poisoning himself seventy times, to discover which plants heal; his materia medica is the root of Chinese medicine.

Zhurong is the god of fire and of the south, who rides two dragons. At the command of heaven he defeated the water god Gonggong, and in some accounts he separated heaven and earth by cutting the link between gods and mortals.

deities.earliest_attestation: Warring States period (Chuci Tianwen, Zuozhuan, Guoyu); fuller myth in Huainanzi (c. 139 BCE) and Liezi
deities.summary: Gonggong, the red-haired serpent-bodied water god, lost his war with Zhurong and in his fury rammed Mount Buzhou, the pillar of heaven. The sky tilted to the northwest and the earth sank to the southeast, which is why the stars move west and the rivers run east; Nüwa had to mend the broken sky.

Chiyou, horned and bronze-headed, with eighty-one brothers, invented metal weapons and waged war against the Yellow Emperor. At Zhuolu he summoned fog and storms until Huangdi's south-pointing chariot and the drought-goddess Ba defeated him. He was later worshipped as a war god and is honored as an ancestor by the Hmong.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ming–Qing period popular scripture and belief
deities.summary: Meng Po waits at the Bridge of Forgetfulness at the end of the ten courts. Before any soul is reborn she gives it her soup of oblivion, so it forgets its past life and enters the next one clean.

alternate_names: Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak
deities.earliest_attestation: Han period (Mount Tai as abode of the dead); imperial title 1011 CE
deities.summary: The Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak lives in Mount Tai, where every soul returns at death. He holds the registers of life and death, oversees the seventy-two (or seventy-six) bureaus of the afterlife and sets the span of each human life.

deities.earliest_attestation: Song period (statue found on Mount Tai, 1008 CE)
deities.summary: Bixia Yuanjun, Sovereign of the Azure Clouds, is the mother goddess of Mount Tai. Women climb her mountain to pray for children and safe births; her attendants include Lady of Eyesight and the goddess who brings sons.

primary_sources: Book of Transformations of Wenchang (Wenchang huashu)
deities.summary: Wenchang, the Emperor-Lord of Literature, is the star-god of culture and examinations. Through seventy-three incarnations he lived as a righteous scholar and official; students pray to him before every examination, and he rewards virtue and learning.

deities.earliest_attestation: Han period (Black Warrior asterism); anthropomorphic Zhenwu from Song
deities.summary: Xuanwu, the Perfected Warrior, rules the north. Once a prince who left the palace to cultivate the Dao on Wudang Mountain, he was raised to heaven and subdued the demon tortoise and snake that now lie beneath his feet. He guards against demons, fire and flood.

deities.earliest_attestation: Tang period (Xu Youguai lu, 9th c. CE)
primary_sources: Xu Youguai lu (Sequel to Records of the Mysterious and Strange)
deities.summary: Yue Lao, the Old Man Under the Moon, binds the ankles of those destined to marry with an invisible red thread. Whatever distance or status separates them, the thread cannot be broken.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ming period as a triad; Shouxing (Canopus) worship from Zhou–Han
deities.summary: The Three Stars are Fu (blessing), Lu (rank and wealth) and Shou (longevity). Shouxing, the Old Man of the South Pole with his tall forehead, peach and staff, is the star Canopus and grants long life; the three stand together on every family altar.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Usa Shrine; Shoku Nihongi, 737 CE)
deities.summary: Hachiman is the kami of archery and war, protector of the nation and guardian of the warrior houses. He is the spirit of Emperor Ōjin, revered with his mother Empress Jingū; the Minamoto clan took him as their ancestral god, and in 781 the court named him a Great Bodhisattva who protects the Buddha's law.

alternate_names: Master of the August Center of Heaven
deities.summary: At the very beginning, when heaven and earth first parted, Ame-no-Minakanushi came into being alone in the Plain of High Heaven and hid his form. He is the first of the kami, the Lord of the Center of Heaven from whom the generative powers unfold.

Takamimusubi, the High Generative Force, is the second of the three primordial kami. With Amaterasu he directs the affairs of the High Plain of Heaven, sends envoys to pacify the land below and commands the descent of his grandson Ninigi.

Kamimusubi, the Divine Generative Force, is the third primordial kami. She revives Ōkuninushi when his brothers kill him, sends the tiny kami Sukunabikona as his partner, and gives the seeds that sprang from the slain food goddess to the world.

Ōkuninushi, Great Master of the Land, healed the White Hare of Inaba, survived death twice at his brothers' hands, endured Susanoo's trials in the underworld and won his daughter. With Sukunabikona he shaped and settled the land, then yielded it to the heavenly kami and withdrew to rule the hidden world from Izumo, where all the kami gather each tenth month to decide human bonds.

Sukunabikona, the tiny kami who came over the sea in a seed-pod boat, is the son of Kamimusubi. He helped Ōkuninushi build the land, taught medicine, hot springs, sake brewing and charms against pests, then left for the Eternal Land across the sea.

deities.earliest_attestation: Heian period (12th c. CE) as a named cult; Hiruko in Kojiki 712
deities.summary: Ebisu, the smiling fisherman with a sea bream under his arm, is the god of fishing, commerce and luck, and the only one of the Seven Lucky Gods native to Japan. At Nishinomiya he is Hiruko, the first child of Izanagi and Izanami, set adrift on the sea in a reed boat, who washed ashore and became the god of fortune.

When Amaterasu hid in the Rock Cave and the world went dark, Ame-no-Uzume danced on an upturned tub, baring herself, until the eight million kami roared with laughter. Curious, Amaterasu looked out, and light returned. Uzume is the ancestress of the shrine dancers and of kagura.

Sarutahiko, the long-nosed, shining kami, stood at the eight-way crossroads of heaven and earth to guide Ninigi down to the land. He is the god of roads, crossings and new beginnings, the leader who goes first, married to Ame-no-Uzume.

Takemikazuchi, the Brave Thunder kami born from the blood on Izanagi's sword, was sent down to demand that Ōkuninushi yield the land. Sitting cross-legged on the point of his sword planted in the waves, he defeated the strongest of Ōkuninushi's sons and secured the country for heaven. At Kashima he pins down the giant catfish that causes earthquakes.

Kagutsuchi, kami of fire, burned his mother Izanami as he was born, and she died of it. In grief and rage Izanagi cut his son apart; from his blood and body sprang thunder, mountain and sword kami. Fire is revered at Atago and Akiba shrines, where people pray for protection against blazes.

Ninigi, grandson of Amaterasu, descended from heaven to Mount Takachiho bearing the mirror, the sword and the jewel, and founded the line of the emperors. Choosing the beautiful Konohanasakuya-hime over her sister Iwanaga-hime, he made the lives of his descendants brief as blossoms.

Kinmamon is the highest god of the Ryukyu kingdom, who comes from Nirai Kanai beyond the sea and from the heavens. He descends at the sacred groves (utaki) to bless the king and the land, and speaks through the priestesses (noro and kikoe-ōgimi).

Shinerikyu is the male partner of Amamikyu. Sent down by the Lord of Heaven, the two built the islands of Ryukyu from stones, earth and plants, and from them came the first people, the ruling lines, the priestesses and the farmers.

Kamuy Fuchi, the Fire Grandmother, lives in every hearth and never leaves it. She is the first to receive every prayer, carries the family's words and offerings to the other kamuy, watches over the household and judges the conduct of its members.

Okikurmi, born of a kamuy and a human, came down to the Ainu homeland to teach people to hunt, fish, weave and pray properly. He defeated demons and monsters, and when the people became ungrateful he left for the land of the kamuy.

deities.earliest_attestation: 7th c. CE (Asuka-period images; Hōryū-ji Guze Kannon)
deities.summary: Kannon is the bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world. In thirty-three forms, with eleven faces and a thousand arms, Kannon answers whoever calls the name, saving from fire, flood, bandits and the sorrows of birth and death. Pilgrims walk the thirty-three temples of the Saigoku route to meet each form.

Jizō, the monk-bodhisattva with staff and jewel, walks the six realms to save beings. He guards children, travellers and the dead; at the riverbank of Sai in the underworld he shelters children who died young from the demons and hides them in his sleeves.

Great King Enma judges the dead. Before his throne every soul's deeds are read from the scrolls and shown in the crystal mirror, and he assigns it to its realm of rebirth. In Japan he is the hidden face of Jizō: the stern judge and the compassionate saviour are one.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Konkōmyō-kyō / Golden Light Sutra transmission)
deities.summary: Benzaiten, goddess of flowing water, music, eloquence, wisdom and wealth, plays the biwa at Enoshima, Chikubushima and Itsukushima. She is the only goddess among the Seven Lucky Gods; as Uga-Benzaiten she wears a white serpent with an old man's head in her crown.

deities.earliest_attestation: early 9th c. CE (introduced with Tendai by Saichō)
primary_sources: Japanese Tendai and Shingon ritual manuals
deities.summary: Daikokuten stands on rice bales with his mallet of luck and his sack of treasures. Once the fierce black protector of the monastery kitchen, he became the smiling god of the harvest, wealth and the household, one of the Seven Lucky Gods; he is also honored as Ōkuninushi.

deities.earliest_attestation: 7th c. CE (Shitennō-ji, founded 593 CE; Hōryū-ji guardians)
deities.summary: Bishamonten, armored and holding a spear and a small pagoda, is the guardian king of the north and the most powerful of the Four Heavenly Kings. He protects the Dharma and the realm, gives victory to righteous warriors, and as one of the Seven Lucky Gods bestows wealth.

primary_sources: Āgama / Nikāya accounts of Brahmā's request (Japanese canon)
deities.summary: Bonten, lord of the Brahma heavens, is one of the twelve guardian devas. When the Buddha awoke and hesitated to teach, it was Bonten who descended and begged him to turn the wheel of the Dharma; he stands with Taishakuten as the Buddha's chief protector.

primary_sources: Japanese Buddhist canon (Śakra in the Āgamas and Jātakas)
deities.summary: Taishakuten rules the Heaven of the Thirty-Three on the summit of Mount Sumeru, holding the vajra. Lord of the devas and of the Four Heavenly Kings, he protects the Buddha and his followers and records the good and bad deeds of beings.

Tenjin is Sugawara no Michizane, the great scholar-statesman exiled to Dazaifu on false charges, where he died in 903. His angry spirit struck the capital with lightning, plague and death until the court restored his honors and enshrined him as a god. Now he is the patron of learning, calligraphy and examinations.
deities.tradition_claim: Enshrined at Kitano Tenman-gū and Dazaifu Tenman-gū; Tenjin worship spans Shinto and Buddhist practice.

deities.earliest_attestation: 10th c. CE (Chinese monk Budai, d. 916 CE); Japanese cult Muromachi period
primary_sources: Jingde Chuandeng lu (Transmission of the Lamp, 1004)
deities.summary: Hotei, the fat, laughing wandering monk with his cloth sack, was the Chinese monk Budai. At his death he revealed that he was Maitreya, the future Buddha, walking unrecognized among people. He brings contentment, abundance and the joy of children.

primary_sources: Shichifukujin popular prints and temple circuits
deities.summary: Fukurokuju, with his towering forehead, staff and scroll, embodies happiness, prosperity and long life together; his name joins the three. He is the Southern Star sage, accompanied by a crane or tortoise.

primary_sources: Shichifukujin popular prints and temple circuits
deities.summary: Jurōjin, the old man of longevity, walks with a staff hung with a scroll recording the lifespans of all beings and is followed by a deer. He grants long and healthy life.

deities.earliest_attestation: Muromachi–Edo period (15th–17th c. CE; group fixed by c. 17th c.)
deities.summary: The Seven Lucky Gods, Ebisu, Daikokuten, Bishamonten, Benzaiten, Fukurokuju, Jurōjin and Hotei, sail into port on the treasure ship (takarabune) at New Year. Gathered from Japan, India and China, together they bring every kind of good fortune.

deities.earliest_attestation: vernacular Korean term; written attestation 18th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: Hananim, the Lord of Heaven, is the highest being in Korean belief, the one Heaven who sees everything, sends rain, rewards the good and decides fate. People turn to Haneullim when all lesser spirits fail.

Hwanin, the Lord of Heaven, saw that his son Hwanung longed for the world of humans. He gave him three heavenly seals and three thousand followers and sent him down to Mount Taebaek, where his grandson Dangun founded Gojoseon.

A bear and a tiger begged Hwanung to become human. He gave them mugwort and garlic and told them to stay out of the sun for a hundred days. The tiger fled; the bear endured and became a woman, Ungnyeo, who prayed for a child and bore Dangun, father of the Korean nation.

deities.earliest_attestation: Three Kingdoms period (mountain cults); Samguk yusa (1281)
deities.summary: Sanshin, the Mountain Spirit, is the lord of each mountain, usually an old sage with a white beard seated beside a tiger under a pine. Every Korean Buddhist temple has a shrine to him. He grants sons, long life and protection, and Dangun himself became the mountain god of Asadal.

deities.etymology: 竈王 (Jowang), the Korean reading of the Chinese Zaowang, "Kitchen King".
deities.summary: Jowangsin, the kitchen goddess, lives by the hearth, honored with a bowl of fresh water placed each morning. She guards the family's food and fire and its fortunes.

primary_sources: Barigongju muga (shaman song of the Jinogwi-gut)
deities.summary: Bari, the seventh daughter thrown away by her royal father for being another girl, was raised in the wild. When her parents fell mortally ill, only she would journey to the end of the world and the land of the dead to fetch the water of life. She served nine years, returned, revived them, and became the goddess who guides the dead and the ancestor of the shamans.
Seongju, the guardian of the house, lives in the main beam. He protects the household and its head; when a house is built or the family moves, the shaman performs the Seongju gut to install him.

primary_sources: Shaman songs of the afterlife journey
deities.summary: Yeomra Daewang, the great king of the underworld, judges the dead in the fifth of the ten courts. Shamans sing the soul's journey to his court, and the living make offerings so that he will judge kindly.
Seonangsin guards the village boundary and the mountain pass, honored at a cairn of stones and a sacred tree tied with cloth. Travellers add a stone and bow as they pass, asking for safe passage.

deities.earliest_attestation: 15th c. CE (Lĩnh Nam chích quái; Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, 1479)
primary_sources: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
deities.summary: Lạc Long Quân, the Dragon Lord of Lạc, son of Kinh Dương Vương and a dragon princess of the sea, rid the land of monsters and taught the people to farm rice, cook and wear clothes. He married the mountain fairy Âu Cơ; their hundred sons are the ancestors of the Vietnamese, and the eldest became the first Hùng King.

primary_sources: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
deities.summary: Âu Cơ, a fairy of the high mountains, married the Dragon Lord and laid a sac of a hundred eggs from which a hundred sons hatched. She led fifty of them into the mountains; she is the mother of the Vietnamese people, honored at the Hùng Temple festival.

deities.earliest_attestation: late 16th–17th c. CE cult; Vân Cát thần nữ truyện (18th c.)
primary_sources: Vân Cát thần nữ truyện (Đoàn Thị Điểm, 18th c.)
deities.summary: Liễu Hạnh, the second daughter of the Jade Emperor, broke a jade cup in heaven and was sent down to earth. She lived human lives, loved, wrote poetry, and returned again and again by her own will, until the court recognized her as a goddess. She is the foremost of the Four Immortals and the Holy Mother at the head of the Mother Goddess religion.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th–17th c. CE (Đạo Mẫu formation); recognized as UNESCO intangible heritage 2016
deities.summary: The Four Palaces are the realms of the Mother Goddess religion: Heaven (Thiên phủ, red), Mountains and Forests (Nhạc phủ, green), Waters (Thoải phủ, white) and Earth (Địa phủ, yellow). Each is ruled by a Holy Mother with her mandarins, ladies, princes and princesses, who descend in turn into the mediums during lên đồng.

alternate_names: Mother of the Mountains and Forests
deities.summary: Mẫu Thượng Ngàn rules the mountains and forests, dressed in green. She protects the hill peoples, the animals and the forest, and grants healing herbs and prosperity to those who serve her.
Mẫu Thoải, the white-robed Mother of the Water Palace, is the daughter of the Dragon King. She governs rivers, seas and rain and protects those who live by and travel on the water.

A boy of Phù Đổng who did not speak or walk for three years rose up when the Ân invaders came. He asked for an iron horse, iron armor and an iron staff, grew into a giant, drove out the enemy, and rode his horse up Sóc Sơn mountain into heaven.

deities.earliest_attestation: early 14th c. CE (d. 1300; Kiếp Bạc temple)
primary_sources: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
Hịch tướng sĩ (Proclamation to the Officers, 1284)
deities.summary: Trần Hưng Đạo, the general who defeated the Mongol invasions three times, was deified after his death as Đức Thánh Trần. He commands the spirit armies against demons and disease; mediums and exorcists invoke him, and his seal drives out evil.

deities.earliest_attestation: folk practice; attested in Lê–Nguyễn period sources
primary_sources: Folk legend of the three Táo (two husbands, one wife)
deities.summary: The Táo Quân are three kitchen gods, two men and a woman, who live in the hearth. On the 23rd day of the twelfth month they ride a carp to heaven to report the family's deeds to the Jade Emperor, and the family sends them off with offerings and paper hats.

Sơn Tinh, the Spirit of Mount Tản Viên, won the hand of the Hùng King's daughter Mỵ Nương by arriving first with the bride-price. When the Water Spirit attacked in revenge, Sơn Tinh raised the mountains higher than the floods, and he defeats him every year. He is one of the Four Immortals.
Thủy Tinh, the Water Spirit, arrived too late to win Mỵ Nương. In rage he raised storms and floods against Sơn Tinh, and every year in the monsoon he attacks again and is beaten back.

deities.earliest_attestation: 17th–18th c. CE (Vietnamese adoption of the Po Nagar cult at Nha Trang)
primary_sources: Tháp Bà Po Nagar temple tradition
deities.summary: Thiên Y A Na, the Holy Mother of Heaven, came to the land as a girl on a floating log of agarwood, taught the people agriculture and weaving, and departed riding a crane. Her temple at Nha Trang draws pilgrims from all central Vietnam.

deities.earliest_attestation: Lê dynasty (15th c. CE) royal investiture of village gods
deities.etymology: Sino-Vietnamese reading of 城隍 (Chinese Chenghuang).
deities.summary: Every Vietnamese village has its Thành Hoàng, the guardian spirit enshrined in the communal house (đình). He may be a culture hero, a founding ancestor or a nature spirit, appointed by royal patent; he protects the village, and his festival is the high point of its year.

primary_sources: Juan de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)
Pedro Chirino, Relación de las Islas Filipinas (1604)
deities.etymology: From Sanskrit bhaṭṭāra / bhaṭṭāraka, "noble lord", via Malay/Old Javanese batara.
deities.summary: Bathala, the Maker of All (Maykapal), is the supreme god of the Tagalogs, creator of earth and of humankind, who governs all things from the sky. He is honored through the anito, the lesser spirits and ancestors who carry offerings and requests to him.

primary_sources: Juan de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)
Pedro Chirino, Relación de las Islas Filipinas (1604)
San Buenaventura, Vocabulario de lengua tagala (1613)
deities.summary: Lakapati is the Tagalog deity of fertility and cultivated fields, invoked at planting with offerings so the land will bear and the people will not hunger. Lakapati joins male and female in one being.

Mayari, the moon goddess, daughter of Bathala, fought her brother Apolaki for rule of the world after their father's death. Apolaki struck out one of her eyes, which is why the moon is dimmer than the sun; reconciled, the two now share the sky, day and night.
Apolaki, the sun god and warrior, son of Bathala, is patron of war and of warriors. He fought his sister Mayari for the throne of heaven, then agreed to divide the sky with her.
Tala is the goddess of the stars and the morning and evening star, daughter of Bathala, who lights the way of travellers before the dawn.

Sitan is the guardian of Kasamaan, the realm of the dead and of misfortune. Four agents serve him, the Manggagaway who brings disease, the Manisilat who breaks families, the Mangkukulam who works fire-sorcery and the Hukloban who can kill with a gesture, leading people to ruin.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1582 CE (Miguel de Loarca, Relación de las Islas Filipinas)
deities.summary: Kaptan is the high god of the sky in the Visayan account of origins. His quarrel with Maguayen, lord of the sea, set sky and sea against each other, and the islands appeared between them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Spanish-era Visayan accounts (17th c.); living oral tradition
deities.summary: Bakunawa, the great sea serpent, rises from the ocean to swallow the moon. In the beginning there were seven moons, and it swallowed six; when it tries to devour the last, people beat gongs and pots to make it spit the moon out. Its appearance marks eclipses.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese/Balinese term; formalized as supreme God from 1959 (Parisada Hindu Dharma)
primary_sources: Parisada Hindu Dharma Indonesia doctrinal texts
deities.summary: Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa, the Absolute Divine Order, is the one God of Balinese Hinduism, of whom all the gods are manifestations. As Acintya, the Unthinkable, he is depicted dancing in flames on the empty throne of the padmasana shrine, beyond all form.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 15th–16th c. CE (Tantu Panggelaran); earlier Old Javanese Shaiva texts
deities.summary: Batara Guru, Lord Shiva as the divine teacher, rules the heaven of Jonggringsaloka over all the gods of the wayang. He commanded that Java be fixed in place by moving the peak of Mount Mahameru onto it, and he decides the fate of gods and men.

deities.earliest_attestation: Majapahit-era temple reliefs (14th–15th c. CE); Javanese wayang
deities.summary: Semar is the squat, pot-bellied servant of the Pandawa heroes, comic and rude, yet he is the god Sang Hyang Ismaya, elder brother of Batara Guru, sent to earth in humble form to guard and guide the righteous. When the gods go wrong, Semar alone can rebuke them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese period; Tantu Panggelaran and Javanese/Sundanese folk texts
deities.etymology: From Sanskrit Śrī, the goddess of fortune (Lakṣmī).
deities.summary: Dewi Sri is the rice goddess of Java and Bali. In the Sundanese tale she was a divine child who died young, and from her buried body sprang rice, coconut and the other food plants. Every harvest begins and ends with offerings to her, and she guards the granary.

primary_sources: Yogyakarta and Surakarta court ritual (Bedhaya Ketawang)
deities.summary: Kanjeng Ratu Kidul, Queen of the Southern Ocean, rules the spirits beneath the waves of the Indian Ocean. She took Panembahan Senopati, founder of Mataram, as her consort and promised to protect his descendants; the sultans of Yogyakarta and Surakarta are her spiritual husbands. Swimmers on the south coast avoid wearing green, her color.

deities.earliest_attestation: Calon Arang text (16th c. CE lontar); Balinese ritual drama
deities.summary: Rangda, the widow-witch queen of the leyak, haunts the graveyard with long tongue, tusks and claws. In the ritual drama she battles the Barong, entrancing the kris dancers to turn their blades on themselves; the Barong's power makes them invulnerable. Rangda is feared and also worshipped as a protector, for her power repels lesser evils.

deities.earliest_attestation: Balinese ritual tradition (attested in colonial-era records; much older)
deities.summary: The Barong, a lion-like protector spirit animated by two dancers, is the king of the good spirits and guardian of the village. In the eternal battle with Rangda neither wins, for good and evil must stay in balance.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese period; Javanese and Balinese wayang
deities.etymology: From Sanskrit Ananta-bhoga, "endless coils", the serpent Ananta.
deities.summary: Antaboga, the great world-serpent, lives in the deepest level of the underworld (Saptapratala) and supports the earth. In meditation he made the World Turtle Bedawang, on whom the world rests, and in one Javanese telling his tears became the jewel from which Dewi Sri was born.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese period; Murwakala ruwatan texts
primary_sources: Javanese and Balinese temple gate reliefs (kala heads)
deities.summary: Batara Kala, the giant born from Batara Guru's spilled seed in the sea, is time the devourer. Batara Guru granted him the right to eat certain people, the sukerta, born in unlucky circumstances; in the ruwatan ceremony the puppeteer recites the sacred words that free them from his hunger. His fanged face guards temple gateways.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ngaju oral chants; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
deities.summary: Ranying Hatalla Langit, the supreme god of the Upperworld, is the hornbill whose union and battle with the Watersnake Jata created the cosmos and humanity. He is the source of life and order, the god to whom Kaharingan prayer ultimately goes.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ngaju oral chants; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
deities.summary: Jata, the Watersnake of the Underworld, is the female counterpart of Mahatala. The two are one divine totality divided into above and below; from their cosmic encounter came the world, and every ritual reunites them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Batak oral tradition and pustaha; recorded 19th c. CE
deities.summary: Mulajadi na Bolon, the Great Origin, is the supreme creator of the Batak. He dwells in the highest upperworld and created the three gods Batara Guru, Soripada and Mangalabulan, who rule the world; his daughter Si Boru Deak Parujar descended and formed the middle world on which humans live.

primary_sources: Penang and Malacca keramat shrine traditions
deities.summary: A Datuk Keramat is a holy guardian spirit, often a Muslim saint, a pious ancestor or the spirit of a place, who dwells at a tree, rock or tomb and protects the land around it. Malays and Chinese alike leave offerings of flowers, fruit and betel at his small shrine; he never accepts pork.

primary_sources: Burmese royal chronicles (Maha Yazawin; Hmannan Yazawin)
deities.summary: Thagyamin, King of the Nats, rules the Tavatimsa heaven and heads the official pantheon of the Thirty-Seven Nats. Each Thingyan (New Year) water festival marks his descent to earth for three days, when he records the good and bad deeds of people in golden and dog-skin books.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (official list traditionally fixed under King Anawrahta)
primary_sources: Burmese royal chronicles (Maha Yazawin; Hmannan Yazawin)
Taungbyone and Mount Popa festival traditions
deities.summary: The Thirty-Seven Nats are the official spirits of the Burmese realm, most of them humans who died violent, untimely deaths, wronged by kings, and became powerful spirits. King Anawrahta set them under Thagyamin to serve the Buddha's religion; spirit mediums (nat kadaw) dance them into presence at the great festivals.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (Thirty-Seven Nats list); legend set in Tagaung period
deities.summary: Min Mahagiri, the Lord of the Great Mountain, was the blacksmith Maung Tint De, so strong that the king of Tagaung feared him. The king lured him with a promise to his sister and burned him alive beneath a saga tree; his sister leapt into the flames. Brother and sister became nats, enshrined at Mount Popa, and every Burmese household keeps a coconut for Mahagiri, guardian of the home.

deities.earliest_attestation: Pagan period legend (11th c. CE setting); chronicles
deities.summary: Me Wunna, a flower-eating ogress of Mount Popa, loved Byatta, King Anawrahta's flower-gatherer, and bore him the two Taungbyone brothers. After Byatta was executed, she died of grief and became Popa Medaw, Mother of Popa, the great nat of the mountain.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th–15th c. CE (mainland Southeast Asian Buddhist art; Pathamasambodhi)
primary_sources: Pathamasambodhi (Southeast Asian life of the Buddha)
iconography: kneeling woman wringing her long hair
deities.summary: When Mara challenged the Buddha-to-be beneath the Bodhi tree, he touched the earth to call a witness. Mae Thorani rose and wrung from her long hair the waters of all the merit he had poured out over countless lives; the flood swept Mara's army away. She is the goddess of the earth and of water offerings.

deities.earliest_attestation: late 13th c. CE (Ram Khamhaeng inscription, 1292: Phra Khaphung Phi)
primary_sources: Tai and Lao household and village ritual
deities.summary: Phi are the spirits that live in the land, the house, the village, the forest and the sky. The guardian of the land (chao thi) lives in the spirit house set before every home and building, receiving daily food, flowers and incense; village and ancestor phi protect the community, while wandering phi of the bad dead must be kept away.

deities.earliest_attestation: Tai/Lao folk ritual; recorded in Thai literary and court rites
primary_sources: Thai and Lao rice-planting and harvest rites
deities.summary: Mae Phosop, the Rice Mother, lives in the rice plant and its grain and holds its khwan (soul). Farmers make offerings to her when the rice is pregnant with grain and at harvest, and call back her soul so that the rice will return the next year.

deities.earliest_attestation: Lao/Thai oral tradition; Buddhist naga lore
primary_sources: Naga fireball (Bang Fai Phaya Nak) festival tradition
deities.summary: Phaya Nak, the naga king, lives in the Mekong and rules its waters. He protects the Buddha's relics and the river people; at the end of Buddhist Lent, fireballs rise from the Mekong where the nagas celebrate the Buddha's return from heaven.

deities.earliest_attestation: Khmer oral and shrine tradition (pre-Angkorian roots)
primary_sources: Khmer village shrine (khtom neak ta) traditions
deities.summary: Neak Ta are the ancestral guardian spirits of the Khmer land, each attached to a place, a stone, a tree, a termite mound or a village. They are the true owners of the ground, honored at small shrines and consulted through mediums before planting, building or traveling.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Po Nagar temple inscriptions, Nha Trang)
primary_sources: Cham and Sanskrit inscriptions of the Po Nagar temple
deities.summary: Po Nagar, Mother of the Kingdom, created the land of Champa, its eaglewood and rice. The Sanskrit inscriptions of her tower-temple at Nha Trang honor her as Bhagavatī, the Goddess, a form of Shiva's consort; she is still worshipped by the Cham as the mother of their people.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Tangaroa, son of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, is the atua of the sea and of all that lives in it. When Tāne separated their parents, Tangaroa's children fled; the fish went to the sea with him and the reptiles to the forest with Tāne, and ever since sea and land have fought. Fishermen return the first catch to Tangaroa.

primary_sources: Māori whare wānanga traditions as published in the 19th–early 20th c.
deities.summary: Whiro, lord of darkness, opposed Tāne at every step. Defeated when Tāne ascended to the uppermost heaven to bring down the baskets of knowledge, Whiro withdrew to the underworld, from where he sends disease and death to consume the bodies of humans.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Tāwhirimātea, atua of winds and storms, alone opposed the separation of Earth and Sky. In rage he followed his father Ranginui into the sky and sent his children, the winds and clouds, to tear down Tāne's forests and whip up Tangaroa's seas. He still makes war on his brothers.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Haumia-tiketike is the atua of wild food plants, especially the bracken fern root (aruhe). He hid in his mother's body from Tāwhirimātea's storm, but his hair showed above the ground and Tū found him and made his children food.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Rūaumoko, the youngest child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, was still unborn at the separation. When the brothers turned their mother face-down so she would not grieve to see her husband, Rūaumoko was left at her breast within the earth for warmth; his stirring makes the earthquakes and volcanic fire.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Mahuika, the fire goddess who keeps fire in her fingernails, lives in the underworld. When Māui put out all the fires of the world and came to her, she gave him nail after nail until, angry at his trickery, she set the world ablaze. Before the last flame died she threw her final nail into the trees, which is why fire can be drawn from wood.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
deities.summary: Kanaloa, god of the ocean depths, of voyaging and of healing, travels with Kāne; together they open springs of fresh water by striking the earth with a staff and drink ʻawa wherever they go. Kahoʻolawe is his island, and the octopus is one of his bodies.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Haumea, goddess of birth and fertility, is the mother of Pele, Hiʻiaka and many gods. She taught women to give birth through the body, possesses the magic stick Makalei that draws fish, and renews herself by returning as a young woman generation after generation.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Milu rules Lua-o-Milu, the underworld beneath the earth, entered through openings at the edges of the islands such as Waipiʻo. Souls who have no ʻaumakua to guide them to the realm of their ancestors fall into his domain.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
deities.summary: Wākea, the Sky Father, mated with Papahānaumoku, Earth Mother, and from them came the islands of Hawaiʻi. From Wākea and Hoʻohōkūkalani came the taro plant Hāloa and the first chief, ancestor of the Hawaiian people; the ali'i trace their genealogy to him.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
deities.summary: Papahānaumoku, Papa who gives birth to islands, is the Earth Mother. From her union with Wākea she bore the islands of Hawaiʻi; she is the foundation on which all life stands.

primary_sources: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Kamapuaʻa, the pig-man god of rain, fertile wetlands and sexual vigor, is a shape-changer who can be a man, a pig, a fish or a plant. He courted Pele and fought her, rain against fire, until the land was divided between them: the wet windward side his, the dry volcanic lands hers.

primary_sources: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Poliʻahu, goddess of snow, lives on the summit of Mauna Kea in her white mantle. She defeated Pele in a contest at the hōlua sledding race; when Pele sent fire, Poliʻahu covered the mountain in snow and froze the lava.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded 19th c. CE (Hawaiian-language newspapers)
deities.summary: Hiʻiaka, youngest and favorite sister of Pele, carried as an egg in Pele's bosom, is goddess of the hula, of healing and of the ʻōhiʻa forests. Sent by Pele to fetch her lover Lohiʻau, she journeyed through all the islands, slaying moʻo monsters and reviving Lohiʻau from death.

primary_sources: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Kamohoaliʻi, elder brother of Pele and king of the sharks, guided Pele's canoe to Hawaiʻi. He protects fishermen and voyagers and can take human or shark form; families who have the shark as ʻaumakua are under his care.

primary_sources: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)
deities.summary: Hikuleʻo rules Pulotu, the paradise and underworld of the Tongan chiefs. When the souls of the high-born arrive, Hikuleʻo receives them. In the Tongan division of the cosmos, Tangaloa holds the sky, Maui the earth and Hikuleʻo the realm below.

primary_sources: George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before (1884)
deities.summary: Saveasiʻuleo, with the upper body of a man and the tail of an eel or fish, rules Pulotu, the Samoan realm of the dead beneath the sea. He is the father of the war goddess Nafanua.

Nafanua, war goddess and daughter of Saveasiʻuleo, rose from Pulotu to free her people of Falealupo from oppression. Covering her breasts with leaves so she would be taken for a man, she won the war and became the supreme authority in Samoa, granting the four paramount titles; she foretold that a new rule would come from the sky.

primary_sources: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)
deities.summary: Tangaloa ʻEitumatupuʻa came down from the sky by a great ironwood tree and fathered with a mortal woman ʻAhoʻeitu, the first Tuʻi Tonga, sacred king of Tonga. Tangaloa Tufunga, the carpenter, cast down chips from his workshop in the sky that became islands.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 18th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: Taʻaroa existed alone in his shell (Rumia) in the endless darkness. He broke out, made the shell the dome of the sky and the earth, and from his own body made the world: his spine the mountains, his flesh the soil, his guts the clouds, his blood the red of sunsets. He created the gods and all things; Taʻaroa is the ancestor of all.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Taputapuātea marae at Raʻiātea (pre-contact); recorded late 18th c. CE
deities.summary: ʻOro, son of Taʻaroa, is god of war, whose cult spread from the great marae Taputapuātea on Raʻiātea across the Society Islands. Human sacrifices were offered to him in war; in peace he is ʻOro of the laid-down spear, and his worship founded the ʻArioi society of performers and priests.

deities.earliest_attestation: Rapa Nui oral tradition; petroglyphs at ʻOrongo; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
primary_sources: Katherine Routledge, The Mystery of Easter Island (1919)
deities.summary: Makemake, creator of humanity and god of fertility, is patron of the Tangata Manu (Birdman) cult at ʻOrongo. Each year he brought the sooty terns to the islet of Motu Nui; the man whose servant first returned with an egg became the sacred Birdman for the year.

primary_sources: E. S. C. Handy, Marquesan Legends (1930)
deities.summary: Tanaoa is primordial darkness and the lord of the sea. In the beginning there was only Tanaoa and his companion Mutu-hei, silence; then Atea, light, rose up and drove out Tanaoa, and Ono, sound, broke the silence. Tanaoa remains god of the ocean and the winds.

primary_sources: E. S. C. Handy, Marquesan Legends (1930)
deities.summary: Atea is light, who rose against primordial darkness and became the sky. With his wife Atanua, the dawn, he fathered the gods and the first people of the Marquesas.

primary_sources: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876)
deities.summary: Vari-ma-te-takere, the Very Beginning, lives at the bottom of the coconut-shell universe in a space so narrow her knees touch her chin. From her own body she plucked her children, Vatea and the other gods, who rose to fill the levels above.

primary_sources: Ulithi and central Carolinian oral tradition
deities.summary: Lugeilan, son of the sky god Anulap, is the sky god of knowledge. He came down to earth, took a mortal wife and fathered the trickster Olifat.

primary_sources: Ulithi and central Carolinian oral tradition
William Lessa, Tales from Ulithi Atoll (1961)
deities.summary: Olifat, son of Lugeilan and a mortal woman, is the trickster of the Carolines. He climbed to heaven on a column of smoke to find his father, survived every attempt of the gods to kill him, gave sharks their teeth and stingrays their stings, and brought fire to humanity by sending a bird to carry it.

deities.earliest_attestation: Chamorro oral tradition; recorded 17th c. CE (Spanish mission accounts)
primary_sources: Spanish mission accounts of the Mariana Islands (17th c.)
deities.summary: Puntan, the first being, before he died asked his sister Fuʻuna to make the world from his body. His eyes became the sun and moon, his eyebrows the rainbows, his breast the sky and his back the earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Chamorro oral tradition; recorded 17th c. CE (Spanish mission accounts)
primary_sources: Spanish mission accounts of the Mariana Islands (17th c.)
deities.summary: Fuʻuna, sister of Puntan, made the world from her brother's body as he asked. Then she turned herself into the rock at Laso Fuʻa in Humåtak, Guam, from which the first human beings came.

primary_sources: Thomas Williams, Fiji and the Fijians (1858)
deities.summary: Degei, the great serpent god of Fiji, lives in a cave in the Nakauvadra range. He hatched the first humans from eggs laid by a hawk and taught them to grow food. When he turns over, the earth quakes; the souls of the dead pass before him on their way to the afterlife, and he decides their fate.

Dakuwaqa, the shark god, guards the reefs and the fishermen of Fiji. He fought every guardian god of the islands until the guardian of Kadavu, a giant octopus, defeated him; he promised in return to protect the people of Kadavu from sharks forever.

Marawa, the spider-friend of Qat in the Banks Islands, also carved people from wood. When he buried his figures and dug them up, they had rotted; so Marawa brought death into the world, while Qat's people lived.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded early 20th c. CE
primary_sources: Tolai (Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain) oral tradition as recorded by missionaries (early 20th c.)
deities.summary: To Kabinana and his foolish brother To Purgo were made by their father drawing two figures on the ground. Everything To Kabinana does is clever and good: he made the useful things, the good fish and the fertile land.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded early 20th c. CE
primary_sources: Tolai (Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain) oral tradition as recorded by missionaries (early 20th c.)
deities.summary: To Purgo (also called To Karvuvu) is the foolish twin who gets everything wrong. Trying to imitate his brother he made the shark, which devours fish and people, and his mistakes brought death, hardship and darkness into the world.

primary_sources: A. W. Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
deities.summary: Daramulan, a sky being of the Yuin and neighboring peoples, presides over the initiation of young men. His voice is the sound of the bullroarer; in some southeastern accounts he is the son or the one-legged companion of Baiame, and he watches from the sky to see that the law is kept.

primary_sources: A. W. Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
deities.summary: Waa the Crow is one of the two great moiety ancestors of the Kulin nations, counterpart of Bunjil the Eaglehawk. Clever and cunning, Waa obtained fire for the people from the women who kept it hidden.

Ngurunderi, the great ancestor of the Ngarrindjeri, chased the giant Murray cod Ponde down the river, and the fish's thrashing carved the Murray's course. Pursuing his runaway wives, he shaped the lakes and coast of the Coorong, then crossed to Kangaroo Island and went up into the sky, where he can be seen in the Milky Way.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
primary_sources: Worrorra, Ngarinyin and Wunambal rock-shelter paintings
iconography: white face with eyes and nose, no mouth
deities.summary: The Wandjina are the creator beings of the cloud and rain who came from the sea and sky in the Lalai (creation time), shaped the land, gave the law and finally lay down in rock shelters, where they left their images. They have no mouths; their power is expressed directly. When the paintings are refreshed, the rains and the increase of life continue.

primary_sources: W. Lloyd Warner, A Black Civilization (1937)
deities.summary: Yurlunggur (Wititj), the great Olive Python of the Yolngu, lives in the sacred waterhole Mirrarrmina. When the Wawilak Sisters camped there, he rose, brought the monsoon storm and flood, and swallowed them; his rising and falling is the coming of the wet season.

primary_sources: W. Lloyd Warner, A Black Civilization (1937)
deities.summary: The two Wawilak Sisters journeyed north across Arnhem Land, naming the plants, animals and places. At the waterhole of the great python they were swallowed in the monsoon storm and later regurgitated; their journey founded important ceremonies and the order of the seasons.

alternate_names: Rainbow Serpent of West Arnhem Land
deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity; recorded 20th c. CE
primary_sources: Kunwinjku rock art and bark painting
deities.summary: Ngalyod, the Rainbow Serpent of the Kunwinjku, is a creator being who shaped the land and its waterholes in the creation time. She lives in deep pools; she punishes those who break the law by flood or by swallowing them, and she brings the rains and fertility.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity; recorded 20th c. CE
iconography: band of lightning arcing around the body
stone axes on head, elbows and knees
deities.summary: Namarrkon, the Lightning Man, brings the storms of the wet season. Stone axes on his head, elbows and knees strike the clouds to make thunder and lightning; his children are the bright orange-and-blue Leichhardt's grasshoppers that appear before the storms.

The Waagal is the serpent creator of the Noongar people, whose winding path across the land made the rivers, lakes and hills of the southwest, among them the Swan River (Derbarl Yerrigan). The Waagal remains in the deep waters and springs and protects them.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity (Arnhem Land paintings); term coined 1926
primary_sources: Arnhem Land and Kimberley rock art
A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, "The Rainbow-Serpent Myth of Australia" (Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute, 1926)
deities.summary: Across Australia, great serpent beings associated with water, rain and the rainbow shaped the land in the creation period and still live in deep waterholes. They give fertility and rain, and they punish those who break the law. Each Country knows its own serpent by its own name: Wunggurr, Ngalyod, Yurlunggur, Waagal and many more.

primary_sources: T. G. H. Strehlow, Aranda Traditions (1947)
deities.summary: Karora, the great bandicoot ancestor, lay asleep beneath the soil at Ilbalintja in the Dreaming. From his navel a sacred pole rose to the sky; from his armpit bandicoots emerged, and later his sons came from his body. When his work was done he returned to rest beneath the waters of the soak.

primary_sources: Charles P. Mountford, The Tiwi: Their Art, Myth and Ceremony (1958)
deities.summary: Purukupali's infant son Jinani died while his mother Bima neglected him for Japara, the moon man. In grief and anger Purukupali refused Japara's offer to revive the child, declaring that from then on all must die and never return. He walked into the sea with his son's body, and the first pukumani mortuary ceremony was held.

primary_sources: Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, vol. 6 (1908)
deities.summary: Bomai came to Mer (Murray Island) from the west in the form of an octopus and other beings, and became known as Malo. Malo brought the law of the Meriam: respect for others' land and gardens, care for the people. "Malo's law" governs land tenure on Mer to this day and was cited in the Mabo case.

facets.facet_name: Revealer of the Eight Trigrams
facets.core_claim: Fuxi read the patterns of heaven and earth and drew the Eight Trigrams, the code of all change, giving humanity divination, writing's forerunner and the order of things.

facets.facet_name: Serpent-Bodied Primordial Pair with Nüwa
facets.core_claim: Fuxi and Nüwa, entwined at the tails and holding set-square and compass, are the first couple whose union re-peopled the world and who measure out the cosmos.
facets.scholarly_note: The brother–sister flood-survivor version is recorded in Tang-era and later sources and in southwest Chinese minority traditions; the Han reliefs show the entwined pair.

facets.facet_name: Judge of the Dead in the Fifth Court of Diyu
facets.core_claim: Yanluo reviews each soul's deeds in the mirror of retribution and sentences it within the ten-court bureaucracy of the underworld, under the authority of the Jade Emperor.

facets.facet_name: The Judge Demoted for Mercy
facets.core_claim: Yanluo first ruled the First Court, but he so often sent the wronged back to life that he was moved to the Fifth; his justice leans toward mercy.
facets.scholarly_note: The demotion tale is recorded in the late-imperial Jade Record (Yuli baochao).

facets.facet_name: The Lord on High of the Shang
facets.core_claim: Shangdi commands the weather, sends blessing or disaster on the realm, and receives the royal ancestors who mediate between him and the living king.

facets.facet_name: Shangdi as Huangtian, Sovereign Heaven
facets.core_claim: Shangdi and Tian are one: the moral Heaven that gives and withdraws the Mandate and receives the emperor's solstice sacrifice at the Altar of Heaven.

facets.facet_name: Mother of the Nine Dipper Stars
facets.core_claim: Doumu bore the stars of the Northern Dipper, the celestial office that records each person's lifespan; through her the registers of fate can be rewritten.
facets.scholarly_note: Her iconography and some titles are shared with the Buddhist goddess Mārīcī, with whom Chinese practice often identifies her.

facets.facet_name: Threefold Emanation of the Dao
facets.core_claim: The one primordial breath of the Dao divides into the three pure heavens and their three lords; they precede and outrank even the Jade Emperor.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Revealer of the Scriptures
facets.core_claim: Before all worlds, Yuanshi Tianzun was; at the start of each kalpa he opens the self-born celestial texts and transmits them downward through the heavens.
facets.scholarly_note: Some medieval Daoist texts identify him with Pangu, the primordial being.

facets.facet_name: Keeper of the Numinous Treasure
facets.core_claim: Lingbao Tianzun keeps the scriptures and talismans of the Numinous Treasure and balances yin and yang between the primordial heaven and the world.

facets.facet_name: Patriarch of Inner Alchemy
facets.core_claim: Lü Dongbin attained immortality through inner alchemy and returns among mortals to heal, test hearts and reveal the way by spirit-writing; Quanzhen honours him as a patriarch.

facets.facet_name: Bestower of Wealth and Prosperity
facets.core_claim: Caishen gathers and dispenses wealth; welcomed at New Year, he rewards diligence and honest dealing with abundance.

facets.facet_name: Magistrate of the Unseen City
facets.core_claim: Each city has its Chenghuang who governs its dead and spirits, records deeds, and escorts souls to the underworld courts, just as the earthly magistrate governs the living.

facets.facet_name: Tamer of Rivers at Guankou
facets.core_claim: Erlang (as the son of Li Bing) subdued the river dragon and the floods of the Min River, giving Sichuan the Dujiangyan waterworks and its fertile plain.

facets.facet_name: Three-Eyed Warrior of Heaven
facets.core_claim: With his third eye that sees through every disguise, his three-pointed blade and his celestial hound, Erlang defeats demons and even the Monkey King.

facets.facet_name: Rain-Giving Sovereigns of the Waters
facets.core_claim: The Dragon Kings govern seas, rivers and rain under the Jade Emperor; their favour ends drought and their anger floods the land.
facets.scholarly_note: The kingly, palace-dwelling form owes much to Indian naga-kings transmitted through Buddhism, joined to older Chinese rain-dragon cults.

facets.facet_name: Yang Counterpart of the Queen Mother
facets.core_claim: Ruling the eastern paradise and the registers of male immortals, Dongwanggong pairs with Xi Wangmu as yang to her yin.
facets.scholarly_note: Scholars generally regard him as a Han-era creation to give Xi Wangmu a cosmological counterpart.

facets.facet_name: Unborn Mother of All Souls
facets.core_claim: "True Emptiness Native Land, Eternal Venerable Mother": she is the uncreated mother to whom all her lost children will return.

facets.facet_name: Mother Calling Her Children Home
facets.core_claim: In the last kalpa the Mother sends Maitreya to gather the ninety-six myriad lost children back to her, ending the cycle of suffering.

facets.facet_name: Ancestral Sovereign and Civilizer
facets.core_claim: Huangdi founded civilized order: he defeated chaos at Zhuolu, established the arts of rule and medicine, and ascended to heaven on a dragon.

facets.facet_name: Yellow Thearch of the Center
facets.core_claim: In the Five Phases cosmology Huangdi is the deity of the center and of earth, around whom the four directional thearchs are ordered.

facets.facet_name: Divine Farmer Who Tasted the Hundred Herbs
facets.core_claim: Shennong gave the plough and the five grains, and by tasting every herb at the risk of his own life revealed the healing and poisonous plants.

facets.facet_name: Fire Lord of the South
facets.core_claim: Zhurong governs fire and the southern quarter and fought Gonggong to keep the waters from overwhelming the world.

facets.facet_name: Rebel Who Broke the Pillar of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Defeated in battle, Gonggong smashed Mount Buzhou, tearing a hole in heaven and tilting the world; floods poured out until the sky was repaired.

facets.facet_name: Rebel War God Defeated at Zhuolu
facets.core_claim: Chiyou forged the first weapons and challenged the Yellow Emperor's order with storm and fog; defeated, he became the patron of war.
facets.scholarly_note: Many Hmong communities regard Chiyou as a revered ancestor rather than a villain; the Han historiographic tradition casts him as rebel.

facets.facet_name: Server of the Soup of Oblivion
facets.core_claim: At the last threshold of the underworld Meng Po gives each soul the broth of forgetting, so that it carries no memory into its next birth.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Mount Tai, Keeper of Life and Death
facets.core_claim: From Mount Tai the Emperor of the Eastern Peak governs the bureaus of the dead and fixes each person's lifespan in his registers.

facets.facet_name: Mountain Mother Who Grants Children
facets.core_claim: From the summit of Mount Tai Bixia Yuanjun grants children, protects mothers in childbirth and heals the sight of the faithful.

facets.facet_name: Star-Lord of Literature and Examinations
facets.core_claim: Wenchang presides over literature, learning and the civil examinations, bestowing success on the diligent and virtuous.

facets.facet_name: Perfected Warrior of the North
facets.core_claim: Barefoot, sword in hand, standing on tortoise and snake, Zhenwu commands the northern heavens and quells demons; Wudang Mountain is his seat.

facets.facet_name: Binder of the Red Thread of Marriage
facets.core_claim: Yue Lao keeps the book of marriages and ties destined spouses together with a red cord that no circumstance can sever.

facets.facet_name: Star-Gods of Blessing, Rank and Longevity
facets.core_claim: Fu, Lu and Shou bring the three goods of life: happiness, success and long life. Shouxing, the South Pole star, decides each lifespan.

facets.facet_name: Protector of the Nation and the Warriors
facets.core_claim: Hachiman, the deified Emperor Ōjin, guards the nation and the warrior clans; samurai prayed to him before battle.

facets.facet_name: Hachiman Daibosatsu
facets.core_claim: Hachiman was the first kami to receive the title of bodhisattva; he protected the building of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji and unites kami worship and the Buddha way.

facets.facet_name: First Kami at the Center of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Ame-no-Minakanushi appeared first of all beings, alone and without a partner, and at once concealed himself; he is the still center from which creation proceeds.
facets.scholarly_note: Barely mentioned in the Kojiki; elevated to supreme creator by Edo-period Kokugaku theologian Hirata Atsutane and by several new religions; medieval practice linked him with the pole-star bodhisattva Myōken.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Generative Force (Musubi)
facets.core_claim: Musubi, the power that ties and generates, is embodied in Takamimusubi; with Amaterasu he governs heaven and orders the descent of the imperial grandson.

facets.facet_name: Generative Power Who Revives and Gives Seed
facets.core_claim: Kamimusubi restores the murdered Ōkuninushi to life and gathers the seeds of the five grains from the body of the food goddess; she is the life-giving musubi of the Izumo line.

facets.facet_name: Builder and Ruler of the Land
facets.core_claim: Killed and revived, tested in the underworld, Ōkuninushi built the country with Sukunabikona and taught medicine and agriculture before ceding rule to Amaterasu's line.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Hidden Realm and of Bonds (En-musubi)
facets.core_claim: After ceding the visible land, Ōkuninushi rules the hidden world (kakuriyo) from Izumo, where the gods assemble to tie the bonds of marriage and fate.

facets.facet_name: Tiny Healer Who Came Over the Sea
facets.core_claim: Small as a seed, Sukunabikona came from beyond the sea, gave medicine, brewing and healing springs, and returned to Tokoyo, the eternal land.

facets.facet_name: Smiling God of Fishing and Commerce
facets.core_claim: Ebisu brings the catch to fishermen and customers to merchants; luck, for him, arrives from beyond the sea.

facets.facet_name: The Rejected First Child Returned as Luck
facets.core_claim: Born boneless and cast away by his divine parents, Hiruko drifted across the ocean and came ashore as Ebisu; the rejected child becomes the bringer of fortune.
facets.scholarly_note: The Ebisu–Hiruko identification is medieval (Nishinomiya); Miho Shrine identifies Ebisu with Kotoshironushi instead.

facets.facet_name: Dancer Who Drew Out the Sun
facets.core_claim: Uzume's ecstatic, laughing dance before the cave drew Amaterasu out and restored light to the world; every kagura dance repeats it.

facets.facet_name: Guide at the Crossroads of Heaven and Earth
facets.core_claim: Sarutahiko waited at the crossroads of heaven to lead the heavenly grandson to earth; he opens every road and guards its crossings.

facets.facet_name: Thunder-Sword Who Subdued the Land
facets.core_claim: Takemikazuchi brought the land under heaven's rule by the power of thunder and sword and keeps the earthquake-catfish pinned beneath the keystone at Kashima.

facets.facet_name: Fire Whose Birth Brought Death
facets.core_claim: Kagutsuchi's birth killed Izanami and opened the way to Yomi; his slain body gave rise to many kami; fire both destroys and generates.

facets.facet_name: The Heavenly Grandson Who Descended with the Regalia
facets.core_claim: Sent down by Amaterasu and Takamimusubi with the three sacred treasures, Ninigi came to earth at Takachiho to rule the land; his great-grandson was the first emperor, Jimmu.

facets.facet_name: High God Who Comes from Beyond the Sea
facets.core_claim: Kinmamon arrives from Nirai Kanai and from heaven to the sacred groves, possesses the high priestesses and blesses the realm.

facets.facet_name: Male Creator of the Ryukyu Islands with Amamikyu
facets.core_claim: With Amamikyu, Shinerikyu raised the islands from the sea at heaven's command and became father of the first Ryukyuan peoples.

facets.facet_name: Hearth Grandmother Who Carries Prayers
facets.core_claim: Every Ainu prayer begins with Fire Grandmother in the hearth, who conveys words and offerings to the kamuy and testifies to the family's conduct.

facets.facet_name: Half-Divine Teacher of the Ainu
facets.core_claim: Okikurmi taught the Ainu the arts of life and the right ways of prayer, guarded them from evil, and withdrew when they grew disrespectful.

facets.facet_name: Bodhisattva Who Hears the Cries of the World
facets.core_claim: Whoever calls Kannon's name in danger is heard and saved; Kannon takes any form needed, monk, maiden, king or god, to reach each being.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of Children and the Dead
facets.core_claim: Jizō descends into every hell, protects the souls of children at the Sai riverbank, and guides travellers and the dead to safety.

facets.facet_name: Great King Who Judges the Dead
facets.core_claim: Enma reads each soul's record and its reflection in the mirror of deeds and pronounces its destination among the six realms.

facets.facet_name: Enma as a Manifestation of Jizō
facets.core_claim: The terrifying judge is Jizō in wrathful guise; judgment itself is an act of compassion.
facets.scholarly_note: The Enma–Jizō honji suijaku pairing is set out in the Jizō Jūō-kyō, a Japanese apocryphal sutra.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Music, Eloquence and Flowing Water
facets.core_claim: Benzaiten gives eloquence, learning and music, protects the realm, and in her island shrines grants wealth that flows like water.

facets.facet_name: Smiling Lord of Rice and Wealth
facets.core_claim: Daikoku's magic mallet shakes out fortune and his sack never empties; he guards the kitchen and blesses the harvest.

facets.facet_name: The Great Black One, Protector of the Dharma
facets.core_claim: Daikokuten began as the wrathful black deva who protects monks and their food; his fierceness softened into abundance.

facets.facet_name: Guardian King of the North
facets.core_claim: Bishamonten guards the northern quarter of the world-mountain and those who hear the Dharma; warriors such as Uesugi Kenshin took him as patron.

facets.facet_name: Deva Who Asked the Buddha to Teach
facets.core_claim: Bonten, the highest of the world's gods, kneels before the Buddha and asks him to teach; even the creator serves the Dharma.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three
facets.core_claim: From his palace atop Sumeru, Taishakuten commands the devas and guardian kings and defends the Dharma against the asuras.

facets.facet_name: Vengeful Spirit Turned Patron of Learning
facets.core_claim: Wronged in life, Michizane's spirit raged as thunder over the capital; enshrined and pacified, he became Tenjin, who blesses students and scholars.

facets.facet_name: Maitreya Walking Unrecognized
facets.core_claim: Hotei's death verse revealed him as Maitreya in disguise; the future Buddha already walks among us, laughing, carrying the world's troubles in his sack.

facets.facet_name: Embodiment of Happiness, Wealth and Longevity
facets.core_claim: Fukurokuju carries in one person fuku (happiness), roku (wealth) and ju (longevity) and grants wisdom with long life.

facets.facet_name: Old Man of Longevity with the Scroll of Lifespans
facets.core_claim: Jurōjin keeps the scroll on which every life's length is written and grants years to the faithful.

facets.facet_name: Gods of Fortune on the Treasure Ship
facets.core_claim: At New Year the Seven arrive on the takarabune laden with treasure; placing their picture under the pillow brings a lucky first dream.
facets.scholarly_note: The membership varied before the Edo period (Kichijōten sometimes replaced Jurōjin).

facets.facet_name: The One Lord of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Above all spirits stands Hananim, Heaven itself as a personal lord, who watches over human conduct and governs destiny.

facets.facet_name: Hananim as the Name of God in Korean Christianity
facets.core_claim: Korean Christians call the one God Hananim (Protestant) or Haneunim, the Lord of Heaven Koreans already knew.
facets.scholarly_note: Adopted by Protestant translators from the 1880s; the Catholic Church in Korea historically used Cheonju (Lord of Heaven) and now also Haneunim.

facets.facet_name: Heavenly Father in the Dangun Myth
facets.core_claim: Hwanin rules heaven and sends his son Hwanung to earth with the three seals to benefit humankind broadly (hongik ingan).
facets.scholarly_note: The Samguk yusa glosses Hwanin as 帝釋 (Jeseok), i.e. the Buddhist Śakra/Indra. Daejonggyo (1909) treats Hwanin, Hwanung and Dangun as the triune Hanul.

facets.facet_name: Bear Who Became the Mother of the Nation
facets.core_claim: Through patient endurance in the dark cave the bear became a woman and mother of Dangun; she is the earthly mother of the Korean people.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Mountain with His Tiger
facets.core_claim: Each mountain has its Sanshin who governs its land and creatures; with his tiger messenger he protects villages and grants offspring and longevity.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of the Hearth and Kitchen
facets.core_claim: Each morning the housewife sets clean water for Jowang, who protects the hearth, the family's food and its luck.

facets.facet_name: Abandoned Daughter Who Fetched the Water of Life
facets.core_claim: Bari crossed into the otherworld, served its guardian and returned with the water and flowers of life to raise her dead parents.

facets.facet_name: Guide of the Dead and First Shaman
facets.core_claim: Refusing worldly reward, Bari chose to become the deity who leads the souls of the dead to the other world; shamans sing her story in every funeral gut.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of the House-Beam
facets.core_claim: Seongju dwells in the ridge beam, the highest of the household gods, keeping the house and family whole.

facets.facet_name: Great King of the Underworld Court
facets.core_claim: Yeomra examines each soul's life and passes sentence; the jeoseung saja, his messengers, fetch the dead to his court.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of the Village and the Pass
facets.core_claim: At the seonangdang by the road, Seonangsin watches the village's boundary, keeping out disease and evil and protecting travellers.
facets.scholarly_note: The name derives from Chinese Chenghuang (城隍), the City God, merged with indigenous village-guardian cults.

facets.facet_name: Dragon Ancestor of the Vietnamese
facets.core_claim: From the sea came Lạc Long Quân, who slew the fish-demon, the fox-spirit and the tree-demon and civilized the people; all Vietnamese are "children of the dragon".

facets.facet_name: Dragon and Fairy Who Parted
